title: Cab Calloway's discipline and power
summary: Jones praises Cab Calloway as a disciplinarian and, he says, the most powerful black man alive, who helped bands travel to Army camps in the war.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: And Fess came into the hotel on Central Avenue — and that's one of the first times in my life — you know, Cab Calloway, people don't know but Cab Calloway would work so much and do so many things off the stage, because Cab Calloway was doing so many civic things that people don't know nothing about. You know, it would take him 2 months and then if he's off for 2 or 3 days he'd get tore up. But then for the next two months he took care of business; he didn't mess around, because you know he didn't go for no namby-pamby. Because you know good and well if you come in there with a stick of pot that was a $25 fine; the next time fired.
The next time, your job. A great disciplinarian. The top band leader in the world as far as I'm concerned.

That's right, fired... He learned it from Mr. Bennie Moten and good gosh and you'd better do and he did it and that was it. He said, "Well, what do I do?" And I said, "Well, Fess, you have to let him go because you have to do this." And here's something that peoples don't know today. I must interject this, which you heard me say a thing when I was with Joe Bushkin when we was with the Jackie Gleason show, that we had some things that you didn't know and I knew. As of today I don't

believe - and I know how powerful the man was - as of today we've had our so-called leaders, and I'm not going with black now, but there is no figure in the Negro world per se as powerful as Mr. Cab Calloway. He has more power structure than any Negro that has ever lived since 1930. He has the political strength; he has the economic strength. But who could he will it to or who could he tell it to? The things that this man has represented, the things that I know that this man did during the War. There was no transportation for no orchestra - they came to Mr. Cab Calloway. They did not go to Paul Whiteman; they did not go to Benny Goodman; they did not go to Guy Lombardo. They said, "Cab, how do we get these musicians transported to play these Army camps?" And Mr. Cab Calloway showed them how. Without Mr. Calloway musicians wouldn't have been able to travel because there was a thing on it. Mr. Cab Calloway, the greatest that ever lived, and today he's the most powerful black man alive.

I'm trying to tell you, and I defy anybody - I got some people that can back me up because they know he's a powerful man.
